questions.q: For a cleanup task affecting only a few hundred records, what does this lesson recommend?
options: A plain, bulkified anonymous Apex script — it's simpler and entirely sufficient at that scale
Always write Batch Apex, regardless of volume
A Scheduled Apex job that runs nightly forever
Manually editing each record one at a time in the UI
questions.explain: At small volume, a straightforward bulkified anonymous Apex script comfortably stays within governor limits and is simpler to write than standing up a full batch class.

questions.q: Why does better bulkification technique fail to fix a cleanup job affecting 80,000 records in one transaction?
options: Bulkification only applies to triggers, never to anonymous Apex
80,000 is below every governor limit, so this scenario can't actually occur
The job genuinely doesn't fit inside one transaction's governor limits (50,000 SOQL rows, 10,000 DML rows) regardless of how the code is written
Bulkification would fix it; the lesson's claim is incorrect
questions.explain: Once the affected volume itself exceeds per-transaction limits like the 50,000-row SOQL cap or the 10,000-row DML cap, no amount of query/DML placement technique helps — the job needs to be split across multiple transactions entirely, which is what Batch Apex does.

questions.q: What are the three methods a class implementing `Database.Batchable<SObject>` must define?
options: init(), run(), and complete()
query(), process(), and done()
begin(), loop(), and end()
start(), execute(), and finish()
questions.explain: Database.Batchable<SObject> requires start() (defines the records to process), execute() (runs once per batch), and finish() (runs once after all batches complete).

questions.q: What does `start()` return in a Batch Apex class, and what is it used for?
options: A List<SObject> containing every single record to process at once
A Database.QueryLocator defining the full record set, which Salesforce then automatically splits into smaller batches
An Integer representing the total record count
Nothing; start() is optional and can be left empty
questions.explain: start() returns a Database.QueryLocator describing the full job's query, and Salesforce automatically divides the matching records into batches, each later passed to execute().

questions.q: What is the honest decision rule this lesson gives for choosing between anonymous Apex and Batch Apex for a cleanup task?
options: Estimate the affected record count and whether the job needs to run repeatably — a small one-time fix favors anonymous Apex, while a volume near or over governor limits favors Batch Apex
Always use Batch Apex, since it's strictly more powerful
Use anonymous Apex for Contacts and Batch Apex for every other object
The choice makes no practical difference either way
questions.explain: The lesson recommends judging by the realistic affected volume and whether the task is a true one-off, reaching for Batch Apex specifically when volume could approach or exceed per-transaction limits.
